title: Caregiving — The Steady Presence
hook: When someone you love is ill, frail or dying, your body becomes part of their care: how you sit, touch, wait and stay can matter as much as words.
why:
Sooner or later, most men find themselves caring for someone: a partner after surgery, a parent with dementia, a child with a disability, a friend who is dying. Caring is physical work. It involves lifting and washing, feeding and walking, and a great deal of sitting beside a bed. It also involves reading a body that may no longer be able to say what it needs, and offering a body that is steady enough to lean on.

Many men feel unprepared for this. They were not taught how to sit with an ill person, how to hold a hand, how to tell when someone who cannot speak is in pain, or what to do at the very end. This chapter covers the men who care; why sitting down changes a visit; what holding a hand can do; how to read pain when words fail; how to match the pace of someone frail; what is known about hearing at the end of life; and how a carer looks after himself. It draws on earlier chapters, from the quiet body in Part VI to the early-warning system in Part II.

teach.p:
Caring is often described as women's work, and women do more of it. But in the 2021 census of England and Wales, around two million men said they provided unpaid care to someone with a long-term illness, disability or problem related to old age, compared with around three million women. Roughly four in ten unpaid carers were men. Similar patterns are reported in many other countries.

Men who care often do so out of sight. A husband nursing his wife through cancer, a son visiting his father in a care home every evening, a father caring for an adult son with a disability: these men rarely describe themselves as carers, and many do not seek help until they are close to breaking. The chapter on burnout in Part II described how that happens.

Caring changes the body. Carers stand and walk more slowly, at the pace of the person they are caring for. They sit for long hours in uncomfortable chairs. They lift, steady and support, and their own backs and sleep suffer. They become expert readers of one particular body, often noticing a change before any professional does.

The figure here walks slowly, head down. It could be the person being cared for, or the man caring for them at the end of a long day. This chapter is for him: about what his body can offer, and what it needs.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men made up only a small fraction of unpaid carers. Census figures for England and Wales show that roughly four in ten are men, though men may be less likely than women to describe what they do as care.

teach.p:
In 2012 Kelli Swayden and her colleagues studied 120 patients recovering from surgery in a neurosurgical ward. On some visits, the doctor stood at the bedside; on others, he sat down. The actual time he spent was much the same. But when he sat, patients estimated that he had been with them longer, and they reported more positive views of the visit.

The finding applies far beyond doctors. A man who visits a sick relative and stands at the foot of the bed, or in the doorway, coat on, is signalling that he is passing through. The person in the bed has to look up at him, and he looms. A man who pulls a chair up to the head of the bed and sits, so that his eyes are at the level of the pillow, is signalling that he is staying. The visit feels longer and warmer, even if it is not.

Sitting also changes what you can see. At pillow height you notice the face, the breathing, the hands on the cover, the small signs of comfort and discomfort that are invisible from the foot of the bed. And it makes conversation possible: a person lying down can talk to someone at their level far more easily than to someone standing over them.

The figure here sits forward, attentive, at the level of someone lying down. It is the simplest change a visitor can make, and many never make it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if patients judged visits by standing and sitting providers the same way. Swayden and colleagues found that they did not, though in a small pilot study of one ward, so the size of the effect elsewhere is uncertain.
teach.pullQuote: Standing says passing through. Sitting says staying.

teach.p:
The chapter on the quiet body in Part VI described James Coan's finding that holding a trusted person's hand reduced the brain's response to threat. In 2018 Pavel Goldstein and his colleagues went further. They gave mild pain to one partner in 22 couples while the other partner either held their hand or did not. Holding hands reduced the pain, and the partners' brain rhythms fell more into step with each other; the more they did so, the greater the relief, and the better the observer read the other's pain.

These were young, healthy couples in a laboratory, and the mechanism is not settled. But they fit what carers and patients have always said: a hand held during something frightening or painful helps.

Ask before you take a hand, or offer yours on the cover and let them take it. Keep your touch steady and still, rather than patting or stroking fast. Hands, forearms and shoulders are usually welcome; for intimate care, explain what you are about to do before you do it. With people who have dementia, approach from the front where they can see you, say their name and yours, and touch gently, because a touch from nowhere can startle and frighten.

The figure here sits by a bed, holding the hand that rests on the cover. Nothing about the scene is dramatic. Hours like this make up most of caring, and much of what helps happens in them.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if holding a hand made no difference to pain or distress. Goldstein and Coan both found effects, but in small laboratory studies of healthy adults, so effects at a sickbed are a reasonable extension rather than a measured result.

teach.p:
People with advanced dementia, after a severe stroke, or near the end of life may be unable to say that they are in pain. Pain that is not recognised is not treated, and it can show up as agitation, aggression or withdrawal that is mistaken for the illness itself.

In 2003 Victoria Warden, Ann Hurley and Ladislav Volicer published a short observational scale, the Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia, known as PAINAD. It asks an observer to watch for five minutes and rate five things: breathing (normal, or noisy and laboured); negative vocalisation (none, or moaning, groaning, crying); facial expression (relaxed, or sad, frightened, frowning, grimacing); body language (relaxed, or tense, guarded, fidgeting, rigid, pulling away); and consolability (no need to console, or impossible to settle). Other scales, such as the Abbey Pain Scale, use similar signs.

These scales are tools for nurses and doctors, and PAINAD was developed with a small group, so it is a guide rather than a gauge. But the signs they list are exactly the ones a family carer can watch for. And a carer who knows the person's baseline, how they usually breathe, sit and sound, is often the first to notice when something has changed.

When you see these signs, especially a change, tell the nurse or doctor, and describe what you saw rather than your conclusion: “He grimaces and pulls his leg away whenever he's moved, and he's been moaning at night.” The figure here is curled and guarded. In someone who cannot speak, this may be the only way pain can ask for help.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if observable behaviour told carers nothing about pain in people who cannot report it. Observational scales such as PAINAD show useful reliability, though they cannot measure pain directly, and agitation has other causes too.

teach.p:
Caring for someone frail asks a man to slow his body down to theirs. Walking at their pace, not half a step ahead and tugging. Waiting while they find a word, a button or a step, rather than doing it for them. Feeding at the speed they can manage. The chapter on fatherhood described scaffolding: doing just enough to keep a child moving. Caring for an adult is often the same, with the added weight of dignity.

Dignity shows in small physical choices. Come down to eye level when you speak. Speak to the person, not about them over their head, even when they cannot answer. Knock before entering. Explain before you touch. Cover them during washing and dressing. Let them do whatever they still can, even if you could do it faster.

Caring is also slow, repetitive and often thankless, and the frustration builds. The chapter on fatherhood described stepping away when anger rises with a crying baby. The same applies here. If you feel yourself snapping, flooding or about to handle someone roughly, make them safe, step out of the room, calm down and come back. Every carer reaches that point; what matters is what happens next.

The figures here walk side by side at a matched pace. With someone frail, that pace is theirs, not yours. Matching it is one of the plainest ways a body can say: there is no hurry, and you are not a burden.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the pace and manner of physical care made no difference to the dignity or wellbeing of the person cared for. The claim rests on care guidance and experience rather than controlled research, and should be read as established good practice.

teach.p:
It is often said that hearing is the last sense to go. In 2020 Elizabeth Blundon, Romayne Gallagher and Lawrence Ward tested this in a hospice in Vancouver. They recorded the brain responses of healthy volunteers and of hospice patients to patterns of sounds, first while the patients were alert and then, for five of them, when they had become unresponsive near death. Several of the unresponsive patients' brains still responded to the sounds in ways similar to the healthy volunteers'.

The researchers were careful: their results cannot show whether the patients were aware of what they heard, recognised voices or understood words. But they give some support to what hospice staff have long advised: keep talking. Tell them who you are. Say what you want them to hear. Read to them, play music they love, talk about ordinary things.

Near the end, the body changes in ways that can frighten people who have not seen them before. Breathing may become irregular, with long pauses, or noisy as secretions gather. Hands and feet may cool. The person may sleep most of the time. These changes are common, and palliative care teams can explain what is happening and what can be done for comfort. Ask them.

The figure here sits still, hands in his lap, waiting. At the end of a life, sitting like this beside the bed, talking quietly or saying nothing, is often all that can be done, and it is a great deal.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if unresponsive dying patients showed no brain response to sound. Blundon and colleagues found that some did, but in very few patients, and the study cannot show whether anything was understood.

teach.p:
Carers wear out. The chapter on burnout described the exhaustion, detachment and loss of effectiveness that come with demands that never stop, and caring for a loved one can produce all three. Men carers in particular tend to carry on alone, see friends less, drink more, sleep badly and say they are fine.

Use the early-warning system from the end of Part II on yourself. What are your own amber signs: shorter temper, worse sleep, more drink, fewer calls to friends, a body that aches from lifting? Who can watch for them? A brother, a friend, a neighbour can be a trusted watcher, and can also take a shift.

Accept help. Respite care, carers' organisations, support groups, a friend who sits with your father for two hours so that you can walk: these are not failures but part of caring well. The chapter on shared activity described how men often accept support most easily side by side. A friend who comes round to help with a job, or takes you to a match, may do more for a carer than any conversation.

And when caring ends, as it eventually does, the body that has been on alert for months or years often collapses into exhaustion and grief at once. The next chapter, on mourning together, is about that time. The figure here sits slumped low. Carers deserve care too.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if carers who accepted help and respite fared no better than those who did not. Research on carer strain suggests that support helps, though the best forms of support vary between people and situations.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Standing, an eye on the time
poseGallery.annotation: Standing says passing through. Sitting at the level of the pillow says staying, and the visit feels longer and warmer.
With someone frail, the pace is theirs. Matching it says that there is no hurry and they are not a burden.

poseGallery.dontCaption: On your phone at the bedside
poseGallery.annotation: Attention is the most valuable thing you can bring to a sickbed. Put the phone away and let your face answer theirs.

caseStudy:
Gary, fifty-eight, visits his father Alan, eighty-four, in a care home most evenings. Alan has advanced dementia and rarely speaks. For the first few months Gary stands at the end of the bed, says a few words, checks his phone and leaves after twenty minutes, feeling useless.

A nurse suggests he pull up a chair and hold his dad's hand. Gary feels awkward the first time, but Alan's fingers close around his, and he sits for an hour. Over the following weeks, at pillow height, Gary starts to notice things he had missed. One evening Alan is restless, grimacing, and pulls his left leg away when the carers try to move him. He moans at night, the staff say, which is new. Gary tells the nurse exactly what he has seen. An X-ray shows a hairline fracture in Alan's hip from a fall nobody had witnessed. With pain relief, Alan is calmer than he has been in months.

Gary does not notice his own decline as quickly. He has stopped going to his Thursday quiz, he is drinking most nights, and he snaps at his wife over nothing. It is his brother who says something, and offers to take Tuesdays and Saturdays. Gary joins a carers' group that meets in a café, where most of the men talk about football for the first half hour.

In March, Alan stops responding. Gary sits with him for the last two days, holding his hand and talking about the fishing trips they used to take, the flask of tea and the one enormous pike. He does not know whether his father hears him. He talks anyway.
observe: Notice how visitors position themselves around a sick or elderly person: standing, sitting, at the door, at the bedside.
Notice your own pace when you walk with someone older or frailer than you, and whether you match theirs.
Notice how people talk to someone who cannot answer: to them, or about them over their head.
If you care for someone, notice your own amber signs this week: sleep, drink, temper, friends.

drills.name: Pillow Height
steps: On your next visit to someone who is ill or frail, pull a chair close and sit with your eyes at their level.
Put your phone away for the whole visit.
Offer your hand on the cover, and let them take it if they wish.
Afterwards, note what you noticed from that height that you would have missed standing.

drills.name: Pain Watch
steps: If you care for someone who cannot easily describe pain, learn the five PAINAD signs: breathing, vocalisation, face, body language, consolability.
Write down what each looks like on a good day for this person: their baseline.
For one week, note any change from that baseline.
Describe any change to a nurse or doctor in terms of what you saw, not what you concluded.

drills.name: Carer's Amber List
steps: Write your own early signs of strain as a carer: sleep, drink, temper, friends, body.
Name one person who could watch for these signs, and one who could take a shift.
Find a carers' organisation or support group near you and save its details.
Tell the person you named what you have written.

drills.name: Words for the End
steps: Think of someone you love who is old or ill.
Write down three things you would want them to hear if they could no longer answer.
Write down a memory you share that you could tell them, in detail.
Consider whether there is anything you could say to them now, while they can still reply.

quiz.q: Someone says that caring for ill relatives is almost entirely women's work, and that few men do it. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right; only a tiny number of men provide any unpaid care at all
Around four in ten unpaid carers in England and Wales are men
Men now provide far more unpaid care than women in most countries
Men only care for others when it is their paid job in a care home
quiz.explain: In the 2021 census of England and Wales, around two million men and three million women reported providing unpaid care. Many men who care do not describe themselves as carers and seek help late.

quiz.q: What did Swayden and colleagues find when a doctor sat rather than stood at the bedside?
options: Patients thought the visit lasted longer and felt better about it
Patients felt the doctor was less professional whenever he sat down
The doctor spent much longer with each patient when he sat down
Sitting made no difference to how patients judged the visit
quiz.explain: The actual time was similar, but patients estimated sitting visits as longer and viewed them more positively. Sitting at pillow height signals that you are staying.

quiz.q: Which set of signs does the PAINAD scale ask an observer to watch?
options: Blood pressure, temperature, pulse rate and blood sugar levels
Memory, orientation, speech and the ability to recognise family
Breathing, vocalisation, facial expression, body language, consolability
Appetite, sleep, weight and the number of visitors each week
quiz.explain: PAINAD rates breathing, negative vocalisation, facial expression, body language and consolability, each from 0 to 2. A family carer who knows the person's baseline can watch for the same signs and report changes.

quiz.q: What did Blundon and colleagues find when they recorded the brain responses of unresponsive patients near death?
options: No unresponsive patient showed any brain response to sound of any kind
All the patients clearly understood every word spoken to them
The patients' brains responded only to music, never to voices
Some still responded to sounds much as healthy people's brains did
quiz.explain: Several unresponsive patients' brains still responded to patterns of sound in ways similar to healthy volunteers'. The study cannot show awareness or understanding, but it supports the advice to keep talking.

quiz.q: Your father has advanced dementia. He has started moaning at night, grimacing and pulling his leg away when moved. What fits this chapter best?
options: Assume it is part of the dementia, since he cannot tell you otherwise
Tell the nurse or doctor exactly what you have seen, as a change from usual
Ask him repeatedly where it hurts until he manages to tell you clearly
Wait a few weeks to see whether the behaviour settles down by itself
quiz.explain: Grimacing, moaning and guarding are signs of pain that people with dementia may be unable to report. Describing what you saw, as a change from baseline, helps staff find and treat the cause.

quiz.q: You have cared for your wife for two years. You are sleeping badly, drinking most nights, snapping at people and have stopped seeing friends. What fits this chapter best?
options: Push on alone, since asking for help would mean you were failing her
Cut back on visits to friends further, so you have more time to care
Treat these as signs of strain, accept help and find carer support
Ignore it, since these feelings are normal and will pass by themselves
quiz.explain: These are classic signs of carer strain, the amber signs from Part II. Accepting help, respite and support is part of caring well, not a failure.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person you have cared for, are caring for, or may care for in the future: a parent, partner, child or friend. Describe how you use your body with them: where you sit or stand, how you touch them, the pace you keep, how you speak to them. What signs of pain or distress do you know in them, and what is their baseline? Then describe your own signs of strain as a carer, and who could watch for them or take a shift.
reflection.guidance: If you are not caring for anyone now, choose someone you are likely to care for, and think ahead. If you are caring now, be honest about your own strain; many carers notice it last. If this reflection brings up grief or exhaustion, take care of yourself, and use the support resources in this app and in your area.

failureMode: The first failure is to visit standing, at the foot of the bed or in the doorway, phone in hand, so that the visit says passing through. The second is to touch without asking or warning, especially someone with dementia, who may be frightened by a touch from nowhere. The third is to miss pain in someone who cannot report it, reading grimacing, guarding and moaning as part of the illness. The fourth is to hurry a frail person or take over what they can still do, at the cost of their dignity. And the fifth is to neglect yourself, carrying on alone until you break. Sit down, hold a hand, watch for pain, match their pace, keep talking, and accept help.
